Blust (2013): One phoneme: Prentice's (1974) *b1/*b2 distinction is rejected as unconvincing (pp. 574-575). Shibata (2025: 30, Table 2.8) compiles the same value.
Blust (2013): Alveolar (p. 558). Dahl's (1976) *d1, *d2, *d3 are rejected (p. 577). Shibata (2025: 30, Table 2.8) compiles the same value.

Blust (2013): voiced retroflex stop, only in final position (p. 554). At least 26 etyma support it: Iban, Malay, the Batak languages and Balinese reflect *-D as -r but *-d as -t (pp. 575-576). Blust finds a single retroflex found only finally uncomfortable and tests the alternative that *-D was *-d and apparent *-d was *-j, which fails for some sets (p. 576); a non-final *d/D distinction is rejected (p. 575). Other systems, as summarised by Shibata (2025): Shibata lists three PAn roots with it (ikuD, NataD, SateD) (p. 30) and disregards it, its roots falling under d, since no Formosan language reflects it differently from d and even the Malayo-Polynesian support is weak (pp. 5, 30-31, 49); Ross (2015) finds it too weakly supported (Shibata 2025: 39); it is absent from the tables for Ross (1992) and Wolff (2010) (Shibata 2025: Tables 2.11, 2.16, pp. 37, 42), and Shibata does not say which Ross or Wolff phoneme covers its roots. Not the same as the D of Ross (2015), which is one of three phonemes corresponding to Blust's d. Not a phoneme of Shibata's system.

Blust (2013): Palatalised voiced velar stop (p. 554), [gy], an "island" with no matching voiceless stop or nasal (p. 579); reflexes in Table 8.27 (p. 578). Shibata (2025: 30, Table 2.8) compiles the same value.
Blust (2013): Voiced velar stop, defended against Wolff (1982, 1997, 2003) with Paiwan and Puyuma evidence (pp. 579-581). Shibata (2025: 30, Table 2.8) compiles the same value.

Blust (2013): Voiceless alveolar affricate (p. 554). Wolff's (1991) analysis of *t and *C as allophones conditioned by stress is rejected (Table 8.23, pp. 559-563). Shibata (2025: 30, Table 2.8) compiles the same value.

Blust (2013): voiceless palatal affricate (p. 554), distinct from *s in only 20-25 languages of western Indonesia and mainland Southeast Asia (p. 563). Wolff (1982) and Ross (1992) would drop it; Blust weighs the arguments (Figure 8.2, p. 563) and concludes that PAN had a palatal series of voiced and voiceless affricates and a nasal, of which *c was the least stable (pp. 566-567); examples include *pacek, *peceq and *qapucuk (pp. 565-566). Other systems, as summarised by Shibata (2025): Shibata counts four PAn reconstructions with it (lecik, pacek, peceq, qapucuk) (p. 30) and does not treat it as a PAn phoneme; its etyma fall under s, since Amis, Puyuma and Paiwan, the only Formosan witnesses, reflect it the same way as s, and its distribution in western Indonesia can be explained by borrowing from Malay (pp. 5, 31, 33, 49). Ross (2015) finds it too weakly supported (Shibata 2025: 39); it is absent from the tables for Ross (1992) and Wolff (2010) (Shibata 2025: Tables 2.11, 2.16, pp. 37, 42). Wolff's own symbol c stands for Blust's s. Not a phoneme of Shibata's system.
Blust (2013): Voiced palatal affricate (p. 554). Dyen's (1951) *z/*Z split is not kept (pp. 577-578). Shibata (2025: 30, Table 2.8) compiles the same value.
Blust (2013): Voiceless alveolar fricative (p. 554), [s], following Ross (1992) (p. 585). Shibata (2025: 30, Table 2.8) compiles the same value.

Blust (2013): Voiceless palatal fricative (p. 554) that became alveolar after *S > h and the rise of homorganic nasal substitution (pp. 585-586). Shibata (2025: 30, Table 2.8) compiles the same value.
Blust (2013): Usually written *H; the only glottal fricative, so written *h; very weakly attested (Table 8.29, p. 586). Shibata (2025: 30, Table 2.8) compiles the same value.
Blust (2013): Non-controversial (p. 581). Shibata (2025: 30, Table 2.8) compiles the same value.
Blust (2013): Alveolar (p. 558); non-controversial (p. 581). Shibata (2025: 30, Table 2.8) compiles the same value.

Blust (2013): distinguished from *n by widely scattered witnesses outside Taiwan (pp. 581-582); in Formosan languages *ñ and *N have merged everywhere except possibly in Tsou and Kanakanabu (p. 582, n. 99). Wolff's (1993) single *ñ split by stress is rejected (Table 8.28, pp. 584-585) and *n, *ñ and *N are kept as distinct PAN phonemes (p. 585); palatals probably did not occur word-finally in PAN (p. 583). Also listed as a PAn protophoneme by Ross et al. (2023: 30). Other systems, as summarised by Shibata (2025): argued for by Tsuchida (1976: 229) from Kanakanavu ŋ and adopted by Blust (2013: 589 as cited by Shibata) (p. 81). Kept by Ross (2015) (Shibata 2025: Tables 2.14-2.15, pp. 41-42). Shibata rejects it for PAn: in Formosan languages about half of the etyma show the reflex of N and the other half the reflex of n, so they are reconstructed with N (ñamuR, qañud, tañam, ñamñam) and n (peñu, bañaw, S[ei]ñaw, teñeb) instead (pp. 32-33, after Sagart 2015); ñawñaw is in his Table 2.9 but is not assigned in the text. Kanakanavu ŋ is a sporadic change that followed the merger of n and N (p. 81), and the ñ of some Malayo-Polynesian languages is left unexplained (p. 33). Ross (1992) and Wolff (2010) have no ñ in the inventories Shibata gives (Tables 2.11, 2.16, pp. 37, 42). Not a phoneme of Shibata's system.

Blust (2013): Supported as a distinct phoneme by hundreds of languages (p. 587). Shibata (2025: 30, Table 2.8) compiles the same value.

Blust (2013): Palatalised alveolar lateral (p. 554); probably a palatal lateral [ʎ], not a nasal: eight of the nine primary branches in Taiwan reflect it as a lateral (p. 585). Shibata (2025: 30, Table 2.8) compiles the same value.

Blust (2013): alveolar flap (p. 554), defended against Wolff (1974) with comparisons such as *rauC, *rawan, *ruit, *kure(n)dut, *periŋ and *samir that no other proto-phoneme explains (p. 587). Also listed as a PAn protophoneme by Ross et al. (2023: 30). Other systems, as summarised by Shibata (2025): Ross (1992) merges it with his d1 (the d of Ross 2015): d1 is found almost only word-initially and r only medially and finally (Harvey 1982), so the two are written as one phoneme (p. 37). Ross (2015) finds d1 morpheme-finally as well, separates the two again and drops r as too weakly supported (pp. 38-39). Shibata: one of four ACD phonemes not well supported by Formosan languages and found in very few PAn reconstructions (pp. 5, 49); he gives no argument of his own, does not say which phoneme covers its etyma, and refers to Liao (2024) (p. 49 n. 3). Absent from the table for Wolff (2010) (Shibata 2025: Table 2.16, p. 42). Not the same as Shibata's own symbol r, which stands for Blust's R. Not a phoneme of Shibata's system.

Blust (2013): Alveolar or uvular trill (p. 554); an alveolar trill is suggested (p. 588). Reflexes in Table 8.30 (p. 588); subscripted *R1-*R4 are rejected (pp. 588-589). Shibata (2025: 30, Table 2.8) compiles the same value.
